outline.chapter_title: The Pump-and-Dump Scheme: Facts and Procedural Posture
outline.description: This chapter introduces the factual background of the case, including the defendants' social media-based pump-and-dump scheme, the charges brought against them, the district court's dismissal of the indictment, and the government's appeal.
subtopics: The defendants and their large social media followings across various platforms
The mechanics of the alleged pump-and-dump scheme: purchase, pump via false/misleading posts, and dump for profit
The indictment charges: conspiracy to commit securities fraud (18 U.S.C. § 1349) and multiple counts of securities fraud (18 U.S.C. §§ 1348 & 2)
Knight's guilty plea and the remaining defendants' motion to dismiss
The district court's dismissal reasoning: failure to allege deprivation of a traditional property interest
The government's timely appeal to the Fifth Circuit

outline.chapter_title: Standard of Review and the Legal Framework of Securities Fraud Under Section 1348
outline.description: This chapter covers the de novo standard of review for indictment sufficiency and the legal elements of securities fraud under 18 U.S.C. § 1348, including the statute's relationship to mail and wire fraud and the two key elements of scheme to defraud and intent to defraud.
subtopics: De novo review of indictment sufficiency and the requirement to take allegations as true
The three requirements for a sufficient indictment: enumerate prima facie elements, fairly inform the defendant, and provide double jeopardy protection
Section 1348's prohibition on schemes to defraud in connection with securities and schemes to obtain money or property by false pretenses
The borrowing of key concepts from mail and wire fraud statutes (Greenlaw)
The 'scheme to defraud' element: material misrepresentation intended to deceive to obtain something of value
The 'intent to defraud' element: intent to deceive and to cause some harm from the deceit
Defendants' concession on deception but challenge to scheme and intent elements

outline.chapter_title: Scheme to Defraud: Distinguishing the Right-to-Control Theory from Fraudulent Inducement
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the 'scheme to defraud' element through the Supreme Court's decision in Ciminelli, explaining why the right-to-control theory was rejected and how the indictment here properly alleges a fraudulent-inducement theory involving deprivation of money or property.
subtopics: Ciminelli and the right-to-control theory: deprivation of potentially valuable economic information
Why the right-to-control theory fails: valuable economic information is not a traditional property interest
The district court's reliance on Ciminelli and why it was misplaced
The fraudulent-inducement theory: using material misstatements to trick victims into handing over money or property (Kousisis)
Why the fraudulent-inducement theory is distinct from and not a repackaging of the right-to-control theory
How the indictment alleges defendants fraudulently induced followers to purchase securities—i.e., to part with money or property
Why the indictment does not run afoul of Ciminelli

outline.chapter_title: Intent to Defraud: Profit Without Net Economic Harm Under Kousisis
outline.description: This chapter examines the 'intent to defraud' element through the Supreme Court's decision in Kousisis, explaining that the fraud statutes do not require the victim to suffer net economic loss and that a defendant's intent to profit through fraudulent inducement is sufficient to establish intent to defraud.
subtopics: Defendants' argument: the indictment alleges intent to profit, not to harm any victim
Kousisis and the fraudulent-inducement theory in the intent-to-defraud context
The Supreme Court's holding that fraud statutes do not require a victim to suffer net pecuniary loss
Why defendants' followers' receipt of market-value securities does not obviate the fraud charges
Rejection of the 'mirror image' requirement: the victim's loss need not equal the defendant's gain (Baker)
The distinction between intent to profit and intent to harm as 'a distinction without a difference'
How the indictment's allegations of pumping and dumping for profit demonstrate defendants 'had money in mind'

outline.description: This chapter covers the court's reversal of the district court's dismissal and the broader significance of the case for securities fraud prosecutions, particularly in the context of social media and the post-Ciminelli/Kousisis legal landscape.
subtopics: The Fifth Circuit's reversal and remand for proceedings consistent with the opinion
The interplay between Ciminelli, Kousisis, and this case in defining the boundaries of federal fraud law
Implications for securities fraud prosecutions involving social media influencers and pump-and-dump schemes
The broader significance: fraud liability where victims receive something of value in return but were induced to part with money through material misrepresentations
The confirmatory role of Seventh Circuit precedent (Smith) applying Kousisis in a similar context
